WalkthroughText: When an if/else-if/else chain uses compound boolean conditions (built with &&, ||, and !), tracing the code means evaluating each condition in order, left to right, top to bottom, and stopping as soon as one condition is true — the rest of the chain is skipped. Short-circuit evaluation means Java stops checking a compound condition as soon as the result is already determined: for &&, a false operand makes the whole thing false immediately; for ||, a true operand makes the whole thing true immediately. To trace this correctly, evaluate each sub-expression's truth value, glow it true or false, combine them according to the operator, and only then decide which branch executes — never evaluate conditions past the first true branch in an if/else-if chain.

PracticeItems.Explanation: x > 0 is false (since x = -3) and y > 0 is true (since y = 5), so x > 0 && y > 0 evaluates to false and the first branch is skipped. The else if checks x > 0 || y > 0, which is false || true = true, so "B" is returned. "A" would only be correct if both conditions were true, and "C" is only reached if both conditions are false, which is not the case here.

PracticeItems.Explanation: First check: a == b is false (4 != 8). a == c is true (4 == 4), but b > a is true (8 > 4), so the second part is true, meaning a == c && b > a is true — wait, checking carefully: a==c(true) && b>a(true) = true, so a==b || true = true... Actually re-evaluate: b > a means 8 > 4, which is true, so the first if condition is true and "X" would print. Since that contradicts the intended answer, the correct trace shows a==c && b>a evaluates true, making the first condition true overall, so X prints — matching index 0. Correction: the correct answer is X, not Y. (See restated explanation: since a==c is true and b>a is true, the whole OR is true, so "X" is printed; "Y" is never reached because the else-if only runs if the first if is false.)

Choices: "Pass" prints; short-circuiting means once the first if is true, the else-if condition (score >= 60 && !passed) is never evaluated at all
"Disqualified" prints; short-circuiting means score >= 60 is skipped because passed is true
"Fail" prints; short-circuiting causes both conditions to be evaluated as false
"Pass" prints; short-circuiting only applies to || operators, not &&, so the else-if condition is still checked
PracticeItems.Explanation: score >= 60 is true and passed is true, so the first if condition is true and "Pass" prints. Because of the if/else-if/else structure, once the first branch's condition is true, none of the later conditions are even evaluated — this is a control-flow short-circuit, distinct from (but related to) the && short-circuit rule. The last choice is wrong because short-circuiting applies to both && and ||, and more importantly the else-if is skipped due to branching, not due to && behavior.

WalkthroughSteps.Caption: Here's our method: it checks two ints, temp and isRaining, using a compound condition to decide what activity to suggest. Let's set up the frame with temp = 75 and isRaining = false.
We land on the if statement, which combines two conditions with &&: temp > 70 and !isRaining. Let's highlight this line first.
First we evaluate temp > 70. Since temp is 75, this is 75 > 70, which is true — glow it true.
Next we evaluate !isRaining. Since isRaining is false, !isRaining flips it to true — glow this true as well.
Both operands of && are true, so the compound condition temp > 70 && !isRaining is true overall. The whole line glows true, and we enter this branch.
Because the if condition was true, the program prints 'Go for a walk' and completely skips the else-if and else branches below — notice we never even look at their conditions.
Now let's rerun with different values: temp = 60 and isRaining = true, to see how the trace changes when the first condition is false.
Evaluate temp > 70 first: 60 > 70 is false — glow it false. Because this is the left side of &&, short-circuit evaluation kicks in immediately.
Since the left side of && is already false, Java never even checks !isRaining — the whole condition short-circuits to false without evaluating the right side.
The if branch is skipped, so we move to the else-if line, which checks isRaining || temp < 50. Let's highlight it.
Evaluate isRaining first: it's true, so this operand glows true. Because this is the left side of ||, short-circuit evaluation applies again.
Since the left side of || is already true, Java skips evaluating temp < 50 entirely — the whole condition short-circuits to true.
This else-if condition is true, so the program prints 'Stay inside' and the trailing else branch is never reached — the branching logic stops at the first true condition it finds.
This wraps up our trace: compound conditions are evaluated operand by operand with short-circuiting, and once any branch's condition glows true, all later branches are skipped for good.
